content: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia is a hereditary condition characterized by elevated levels of cholesterol and triglycerides in the blood. This disorder is primarily caused by an accumulation of chylomicrons and intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL). It is also referred to as broad beta disease or dysbetalipoproteinemia. The most common genetic cause is the presence of the ApoE E2/E2 genotype, which leads to cholesterol-rich very low-density lipoproteins (β-VLDL). This condition affects approximately 0.2% of the population. Hyperlipoproteinemia type III, another name for dysbetalipoproteinemia, is a rare genetic disorder involving the improper metabolism of lipids, specifically cholesterol and triglycerides. This results in the abnormal accumulation of lipids in the body, a condition known as hyperlipidemia. Affected individuals may develop yellowish, lipid-filled bumps or plaques on the skin, called xanthomas. Additionally, fatty deposits may accumulate in blood vessels, leading to atherosclerosis, which can obstruct blood flow and result in coronary heart disease or peripheral vascular disease. Most cases of hyperlipoproteinemia type III are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. This means that two copies of the defective gene, one from each parent, are required for the disorder to manifest. If an individual inherits one normal gene and one defective gene, they will be a carrier without symptoms. The risk of two carrier parents having an affected child is 25% with each pregnancy. The chance of having a child who is a carrier is 50%, while the likelihood of having a child with two normal genes is 25%. The condition is linked to defects in the gene responsible for apolipoprotein E (ApoE), which is located on chromosome 19q13. ApoE plays a critical role in transporting cholesterol and other fats in the body and clearing fats from the bloodstream. The gene exists in several forms (alleles), with the three most common being E2, E3, and E4. ApoE3 is considered the normal form, while others are considered mutations. Most cases of hyperlipoproteinemia type III result from inheriting two ApoE2 alleles. ApoE2 clears dietary fats more slowly than ApoE3. However, the presence of two ApoE2 alleles alone does not usually cause symptoms; fewer than 10% of individuals with this genetic makeup develop symptoms. Additional genetic, environmental, or hormonal factors, such as hypothyroidism, diabetes, obesity, or low estrogen levels in postmenopausal women, may contribute to the development of the disorder. Rare variants of the ApoE gene, inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, can also cause hyperlipoproteinemia type III. In these cases, only one copy of the abnormal gene is needed for the disorder to manifest. Symptoms may appear from birth, and the severity of the condition can be influenced by additional genetic, environmental, and hormonal factors. Symptoms of hyperlipoproteinemia type III typically develop after the age of 20. Yellow fatty deposits, known as xanthomas, may appear on the eyelids, palms, soles, or tendons of the knees and elbows. Atherosclerosis is a common complication, leading to early chest pain (angina) or reduced blood flow to specific areas of the body, which can cause transient ischemic attacks or peripheral artery disease. Diagnosis of hyperlipoproteinemia type III involves a thorough clinical evaluation, detailed patient history, and identification of characteristic findings such as xanthoma striata palmaris. Laboratory tests may reveal elevated cholesterol and triglyceride levels after fasting, increased very low-density lipoproteins (VLDLs), and an abnormal VLDL-to-plasma triglyceride ratio. Electrophoresis, a laboratory technique that separates proteins by molecular size, can demonstrate abnormal lipoproteins. Genotyping can confirm the presence of two ApoE2 alleles, which, in combination with characteristic symptoms, is diagnostic of the condition. Treatment primarily involves dietary modifications, including a low-cholesterol and low-saturated-fat diet, which can prevent xanthomas and reduce blood lipid levels. Regular exercise may also help lower lipid levels. If dietary changes are insufficient, medications such as niacin, gemfibrozil, clofibrate, or lovastatin may be prescribed. However, drugs like cholestyramine and colestipol are not effective and may increase beta-lipoprotein levels. In some cases, xanthomas can be surgically removed. Estrogen therapy may benefit postmenopausal women by improving lipid clearance. Genetic counseling is recommended for affected individuals and their families. The prognosis for individuals with hyperlipoproteinemia type III is generally favorable with treatment, as most people experience significant reductions in lipid levels. However, untreated individuals are at increased risk for complications such as heart attack, stroke, peripheral vascular disease, intermittent claudication, and gangrene of the lower extremities. Preventive measures include screening family members of affected individuals for early detection and treatment. Early intervention and avoidance of other risk factors for vascular disease, such as smoking, are crucial to preventing complications like heart attacks, strokes, and blocked blood vessels.
